blocks.text: Setting aside these trifles, then, I observe that the Chaldeans sometimes prefix the word son or daughter to the names of birds without any regard to age. Thus in Levit. IX, 13. בר גזא bar geza, or son of geza, is the griffon in Jonathan and in the Jerusalem translator: בר גזא bar geza, that is, son of strength. For elsewhere the griffon is called עזא from strength, and we have shown elsewhere that the letter Ajin, or Gain, is often changed into Gimel. And in Deut. XIV, 13. בת כנפא, daughter of the wing, is the vulture in Onkelos. That the white hawk is called by the Talmudists בר חוריא bar churja, son of whiteness, we show in the last chapter of this book. And in the Talmudic Tractate Bechoroth ch. 9, fol. 57b, בר יוכני bar jucne, or son of jucne, is a fabulous bird of prodigious size (like the رخ [rukh] ruch of the Arabs), which is so called from its lofty nest. For among the Chaldeans יוכני jucne is the same [II, 828] as وكنة [wakna] vvacna among the Arabs, by which they denote not just any nest, but a nest on a mountain or rock. Accordingly we read there: ונפלה ביצת בר יוכני, And the egg of the son of jucne fell; that is, from the summit of a mountain or rock. Now if anyone wishes to learn what destruction the fall of that egg caused, let him read what immediately follows: וטבעה ששים כרכים ושברה שלוש מאות ארזים, And it submerged six hundred villages and broke three hundred cedars. Nor did God create so great a bird for nothing. For it is being reserved, if we believe Elias (not the Tishbite, but the author of the THISBI), לעשות ממנו סעודה לצדיקים עם הלויתן ושור הבר, to prepare a banquet for the righteous, from that bird as well as from Leviathan and the wild ox. But this in passing.

The same manner of speaking is also in use among the Arabs, who call the duck ابن الما [ibn al-mā] son of water; and the raven ابن داية [ibn dāya] son of the withers, because it gladly settles on the necks of beasts of burden that the yoke or loads have chafed and ulcerated, in order to gnaw away the dead flesh. And the thos [jackal] ابن اوي [ibn āwā] son of avvi, or of barking, because in Syria and Cilicia the fields resound with its barking at night. And the beech marten (in French fouine) ابن مقرض [ibn miqraḍ] son of gnawing; and the common weasel ابن عرس [ibn ʿirs] son of the wedding, from its elegance and neat fur; just as in Italian it is called donnola, as if dominula [little lady], and in French belette, as if you said bellula [pretty little one], and in vulgar Greek νυμφίτζα [nymphitza] or νυφίτζα [nyphitza]. Since this word is plainly barbarous, I cannot guess how it crept into Diodorus, in whom you may read, book 1, p. 52 of the edition of Henri Estienne, that the Egyptians greatly venerate certain animals not only living but also dead, οἷον τοὺς τε αἰλούρους, καὶ τοὺς ἰχνεύμονας, καὶ νυφίτζας, καὶ κύνας [hoion tous te ailourous, kai tous ichneumonas, kai nyphitzas, kai kynas], such as cats, and ichneumons, and weasels, and dogs. The flea, too, is in Arabic ابن طامر [ibn ṭāmir] the leaping son. And the sea creatures of female form which they say are found in the Adriatic Sea near Greece they call بنات الروم [banāt al-Rūm] daughters of the Greeks: as they call بنات وردان [banāt wardān] daughters of vardan those little creatures which Dioscorides names κουβαρίδας [koubaridas], Marcellus Empiricus cutiones, and we cloportes [woodlice]; although others understand σίλφας [silphas], or blattae [cockroaches]. But I think the former is truer, and that vardan was formed from the Greek word κουβάριδες [koubarides], with the first syllable cut off.
